1. INTRODUCTION

1.1. I, Mehmet Bagbozan, present this consolidated statement of claim against the Respondent, The Co-operative Group Limited, pursuant to my claims of:

Unfair dismissal under the Employment Rights Act 1996
Wrongful dismissal (breach of contract)
Direct discrimination based on religion and belief (Muslim) under the Equality Act 2010
Direct discrimination based on sexual orientation (gay) under the Equality Act 2010
Victimization under Section 27 of the Equality Act 2010
Procedural unfairness contrary to ACAS Code of Practice

1.2. This statement consolidates the essential facts, legal framework, and specific disclosure requests necessary for proper determination of my claims.

2. FACTS AND LEGAL CLAIMS
2.1 Procedural Flaws in Investigation and Disciplinary Process

2.1.1. Conflict of Interest and Procedural Irregularities

The investigation into both disciplinary processes (ER REF: 698645 and ER REF: 703468) was fundamentally compromised by conflicts of interest:
Pankaj Patel conducted the investigation meeting on 29/07/2024 without prior notice
Gaurang Patel (son of Pankaj Patel) served as note-taker in the first investigation
No neutral third party was present during either investigation
This family relationship created an inherent conflict contrary to ACAS guidelines and likely violated the Respondent's Working with Relatives Policy

2.1.2. Premature Action and Rushed Process

I was suspended within two hours of the investigation meeting on 29/07/2024
The disciplinary meeting was initially scheduled for 01/08/2024, allowing inadequate preparation time
Despite providing a valid sick note from Dr. Kevin Xu covering 01/08/2024 to 15/08/2024, the Respondent proceeded with a rescheduled disciplinary meeting on 12/08/2024
This contravenes Section 2 of the ACAS Code of Practice requiring reasonable time for preparation

2.1.3. Failure to Consider Medical Evidence

The Respondent disregarded my documented medical condition of "Stress at work and anxiety"
My dismissal occurred while I was certified as unfit for work
This violates the ACAS guidelines on considering health factors during disciplinary processes
2.2 Discriminatory Treatment Based on Protected Characteristics

2.2.1. Inconsistent Application of Disciplinary Procedures

As the only gay Turkish Muslim employee, I was subjected to disproportionate scrutiny and disciplinary action
Comparators without my protected characteristics received different treatment:
Key Management: Leila (Muslim) and Gaurang Patel (non-Muslim, non-gay) both mishandled high-value items and keys without disciplinary consequences
Health and Safety: Pankaj Patel found expired pizzas and Leila mishandled chilled food without investigation
Store Devices: Melania, Leila, Pankaj Patel, and Abdullah all took store devices home (admitted in WhatsApp) without disciplinary action
Smoking Policy: Gaurang Patel, Melania, Leila, Abdullah, and JaksKumar Patel all violated the smoking policy without consequences

2.2.2. Selective Enforcement of Policies

The pattern of enforcement reveals that I, as the only employee with these combined protected characteristics, was held to a different standard
The evidence demonstrates prima facie discrimination under Section 13 of the Equality Act 2010, shifting the burden of proof to the Respondent to prove no discrimination occurred
2.3 Specific Incidents Leading to Dismissal

2.3.1. Parcel Incident (23 July 2024)

The disciplinary outcome characterized my handling of an abandoned parcel as "theft"
However:
The parcel had remained uncollected for an extended period
Gaurang Patel demonstrated prior knowledge of the parcel's contents (color, brand) when inquiring about it
No formal parcel handling procedure was consistently enforced
The disciplinary process failed to investigate whether Royal Mail had actually requested the parcel's return

2.3.2. Smoking Policy Violation (26 July 2024)

I took a single inadvertent puff on my vape during my break
This was detected only through targeted CCTV surveillance
Multiple other employees (Gaurang Patel, Melania, Leila, Abdullah, JaksKumar Patel) routinely smoked near entrances or on premises without any disciplinary consequences
The selective enforcement of this policy supports my claim of discriminatory treatment
2.4 Victimization Following Protected Acts

2.4.1. Increased Scrutiny After First Disciplinary Challenge

After the first disciplinary process (ER REF: 698645), I challenged the fairness of the procedure
Following this protected act, I experienced intensified monitoring and surveillance
Minor incidents were escalated rapidly to gross misconduct
This pattern establishes victimization under Section 27 of the Equality Act 2010

2. Case Management Summary

Case Name: Mehmet Bagbozan v The Co-operative Group Ltd
Case Number: 2225465/2024

Unfair and wrongful dismissal
Discrimination based on religion (Muslim) and sexual orientation (gay)
Victimization following protected acts
Disability discrimination (stress and anxiety)

3. Case Principles

Applicable Laws & Regulations:

Employment Rights Act 1996 (unfair dismissal provisions)
Equality Act 2010, Sections 13, 15, 20, 21, and 27
ACAS Code of Practice on Disciplinary and Grievance Procedures

Key Arguments:

Procedural Unfairness:

Investigation conducted with inherent conflict of interest (father-son relationship between investigator Pankaj Patel and note-taker Gaurang Patel)
Disciplinary meeting conducted while on certified sick leave
Inadequate notice for meetings and opportunity to prepare defense
Failure to follow ACAS guidelines

Discriminatory Treatment:

As the only gay Turkish Muslim employee, I was subjected to differential treatment
Comparable misconduct by employees without my protected characteristics was treated more favorably
Evidence shows pattern of selective policy enforcement

Victimization:

Following my challenge to the first disciplinary process, I experienced increased scrutiny
Minor infractions were escalated to gross misconduct level
Pattern of targeted monitoring not applied to other employees

Precedent Support:

Hendricks v Commissioner of Police for the Metropolis [2002] EWCA Civ 1686 (discrimination as a continuing act)
Igen v Wong [2005] EWCA Civ 142 (burden of proof in discrimination cases)
BS v Dundee City Council [2013] CSIH 91 (dismissal during sickness absence)

Human: <file absolutePath='FINALISED 4 FILES/SIMILAR CASES/2 Hesham_Elhalabi_v_Avis_Budget_UK_Ltd__2025__EAT_11.pdf' />: how do you relevant to my case. use tbelow explabantion 1. The Standard Citation Format

For the first mention of a case, use a full citation. Afterward, you can use a shorter, abbreviated form.

Full Citation: Use the format: Case Name \\[Year\\] Court/Tribunal Citation Number.

Example: Watson v University of Strathclyde \\[2017\\] UKEAT 0328_16_0706

Example: Royal Mail Group Ltd v Jhuti \\[2017\\] EWCA Civ 1632

Short Citation: After the first full citation, you can simply refer to the case by name or a shortened form.

Example: "The principle from Watson..."

Example: "...as established in Jhuti..."

Citing a Specific Paragraph: To make your argument even more precise, cite the specific paragraph number that contains the principle you are relying on. This saves the Judge from having to read the entire case to find your point.

Example: "The EAT held that apparent bias is established where a 'fair-minded and informed observer would conclude there was a real possibility of bias' (Watson, para 27)."

Example: "The Supreme Court in Jhuti clarified that a dismissal is unfair if a decision-maker is manipulated by a manager with an unfair, hidden motive (Jhuti, para 18)."

2\. Strategic Placement and Explanation

Citing cases is about more than just listing them; it's about telling the Judge precisely why they matter to your situation.

In Your Written Submissions:

Integrate the case law into your arguments to provide a legal foundation for every flaw you identify. Don't just make a statement; make a statement with a legal reference.

Example:

"The first investigation was tainted by apparent bias due to the father-son relationship of Pankaj and Gaurang Patel, in violation of the principles set out in Watson v University of Strathclyde \\[2017\\] UKEAT 0328_16_0706."

"This is a fundamental breach of procedural fairness and renders the investigation, and subsequent dismissal, invalid."

In Your Evidence Bundle:

Include a separate section in your evidence bundle for "Legal Authorities" or "Relevant Case Law."

Put a copy of each case report in this section, clearly tabbed and indexed.

This ensures the Judge has immediate access to the full text of the cases you are relying on.

3\. The Key Principle: Link it to the Facts

The most effective way to cite a case is to explicitly connect its principle to the facts of your own situation.

Instead of: "I was treated inconsistently, like in the Bessong case."

Do this: "The Respondent's decision to issue a written warning to me for the keys incident, while only giving Gaurang Patel a verbal warning for an identical infraction, is a clear example of inconsistent application of disciplinary procedures. This renders my dismissal unfair, as established in the case of Bessong v Pennine Care NHS Foundation Trust, which held that inconsistent treatment can make a dismissal fall outside the range of reasonable responses."

This systematic approach of citing cases will make your arguments professional, legally robust, and easy for the Tribunal Judge to follow and accept.

## **CASE SUMMARY: Hesham Elhalabi v Avis Budget UK Ltd [2025] EAT 11**

### **What Happened - The Facts**

Mr. Elhalabi was employed by Avis Budget UK Ltd. In April 2019, he was accused of two initial acts of misconduct:
1. **Failing to work at another outlet when instructed**
2. **Leaving an outlet unmanned and unlocked** (disputed duration: 30 seconds vs 2 minutes)

**The CCTV Incident:** While off sick (from 15 April 2019), Elhalabi **obtained CCTV footage without authorisation** on 18 April 2019 to prove he hadn't left the outlet unmanned. When questioned during the investigation on 25 April 2019, he **refused to explain how he obtained the CCTV footage**.

**The Critical Dishonesty:** When pressed for an explanation, Elhalabi claimed **a former employee had obtained the CCTV footage for him**. The employer investigated this claim by contacting the former employee, **who denied any involvement**. This led to a finding of **dishonesty** - the primary reason for dismissal.

## I. CLEANED DATA SUMMARY

## III. LEGAL ANALYSIS

### Procedural Flaws Under Turkish Labor Law

1. **Inadequate Notice and Opportunity to Prepare Defense**:
   - Turkish Labor Law establishes the right to a fair process and defense
   - Employees were given only 30 minutes notice before the investigation and questioning began
   - This severely limited their ability to prepare a defense or seek legal counsel in advance

2. **Improper Suspension Procedures**:
   - Multiple employees, including managers, were suspended without proper justification
   - The suspensions appear to have been implemented without following proper disciplinary procedures under Turkish Labor Law
   - Employees were not provided with a formal opportunity to defend themselves before suspension

3. **Obstruction of Legal Representation**:
   - Employees were initially questioned without their legal counsel present
   - The employees' lawyer was only informed about 2 hours after questioning began
   - This potentially violates Article 49 of the Turkish Constitution which guarantees the right to legal representation

### Potential Violations of Turkish Employment Regulations

1. **Personal Data Protection (KVKK) Violations**:
   - Employees were allegedly pressured to sign KVKK consent documents
   - Consent obtained under pressure may be invalid under Turkish law
   - The seizure and examination of personal data from company and personal devices without proper consent may violate KVKK
   - Article 5 of KVKK requires that consent be "explicit, specific, and freely given"

2. **Privacy Rights Infringements**:
   - Confiscation of devices and accessing personal communications may violate:
     - Turkish Penal Code Article 134 (violation of privacy)
     - Turkish Penal Code Article 132 (violation of secrecy of correspondence)
   - Even on company devices, employees have certain privacy rights under Turkish law

3. **Employment Contract Violations**:
   - Sudden suspension without following proper procedures may constitute a breach of employment contracts
   - Blocking access to work systems without due process may violate contractual obligations

### Communication Patterns Suggesting Bias or Inconsistencies

1. **Misrepresentation of the Investigation's Purpose**:
   - The investigation was initially presented as a "financial planning" meeting
   - This misrepresentation suggests a deliberate attempt to catch employees off-guard
   - Such tactics undermine trust and may be considered a form of intimidation

2. **Potential Conflict of Interest with Investigating Parties**:
   - HIS Turkey employees raised concerns that Paksoy Law Firm also provides legal consultancy to Jules Verne MICE Business Travel, allegedly a major competitor of HIS Turkey
   - This creates a potential conflict of interest that could compromise the investigation's integrity
   - The dual role could risk exposure of HIS Turkey's trade secrets and confidential business information to a competitor

3. **Disproportionate and Potentially Intimidating Measures**:
   - The scale and manner of the investigation (confiscation of devices, immediate suspensions) appears disproportionate
   - Employees reported feeling intimidated and under psychological pressure
   - These patterns suggest the possibility of bias against HIS Turkey management

### Quality and Consistency of Documentation

1. **Formal Documentation Issues**:
   - The "Internal Investigation Notice" was sent only 30 minutes before the investigation began
   - This timing raises questions about the notice's true purpose as an informational document
   - The "Document Preservation Notice" was issued after devices had already been confiscated, creating inconsistency in the process

2. **KVKK Consent Documentation Problems**:
   - Consent documents were reportedly presented under circumstances that may invalidate them
   - Turkish contract law requires that consent be given freely and without duress
   - The timing and manner of obtaining signatures raise significant concerns about the documents' validity

3. **Lack of Transparency in Investigation Documentation**:
   - The specific allegations were not clearly documented or communicated to the affected employees
   - This lack of specificity hampers the ability of employees to defend themselves effectively

## IV. COMPREHENSIVE FINDINGS

### Cleaned Data Summary Findings

1. HIS Travel Turkey has been a successful and award-winning branch of the global HIS Travel network, operating in Turkey since 2005 and overseeing operations in multiple countries.

2. The internal investigation stemmed from a whistleblower report alleging conflicts of interest, expense management issues, and third-party management irregularities.

2. The sequence of events shows an escalating pattern of control measures: from confiscation of devices to suspension of employees and restrictions on communication.

3. The timeline reveals a concerning lack of opportunity for affected employees to prepare their defense or seek proper legal counsel before questioning.

### Legal Analysis Findings

2. Significant data privacy concerns arise from the manner in which personal information was accessed and devices were confiscated, potentially violating KVKK and relevant provisions of the Turkish Penal Code.

3. The investigation's execution shows patterns that could be interpreted as intimidation, particularly in the pressure allegedly applied to sign documentation and the psychological aspects of the questioning procedures.

### Overall Conclusion

The internal investigation at HIS Travel Turkey appears to have been conducted in a manner that raises substantial concerns regarding procedural fairness, legal compliance, and employee rights protection. While the investigation may be based on legitimate concerns (the whistleblower allegations), the execution of the investigation process shows numerous potential violations of Turkish employment law and data protection regulations.

The lack of transparency, limited opportunity for defense, and potential conflicts of interest with the investigating parties further compromise the investigation's integrity. These issues may expose HIS Co. Ltd. to legal liability under Turkish law and damage employee relations within the organization.

This analysis identifies a clear need for an impartial review of the investigation process itself to ensure compliance with Turkish legal requirements and to protect both the company's interests and employee rights.

Its primary application, as previously discussed, is to "glue" the kick and bass, creating the characteristic "groove pumping" effect.9 This ensures the kick drum has its own distinct space in the low end and enhances the rhythmic drive of the track. Reverb and delay effects should be sidechained, triggered by the main vocals (to be added later) and lead instruments.54 This technique dynamically "ducks" the wet effects when the dry signal is present, ensuring that vocals and leads remain "front and center in mix" and cut through clearly without being drowned in effects.57 This is achieved by setting up the reverb/delay on auxiliary (bus) tracks, and then placing a compressor after the effect on the aux track, with the dry vocal/lead as the sidechain input.57Sidechain compression is not a singular effect but a versatile dynamic tool. Its applications range from rhythmic emphasis on the low end to enhancing vocal intelligibility. Mastering these dual applications and tailoring the compressor's attack, release, threshold, and ratio settings for each specific use case is crucial for achieving a professional, dancefloor-ready mix where all elements have their space and impact without masking each other.Dynamics: Sculpting Energy with Group Bus Compression and AutomationEffective dynamic control is paramount for shaping the emotional arc and dancefloor energy of the track. Executive Summary

AI Drive (formerly AI PDF) is a document‑management SaaS platform that allows users to upload, search and analyse large collections of PDFs, Word documents and other files using generative‑AI models (OpenAI, Anthropic and Google models). It differentiates itself from native ChatGPT file uploads by permitting thousands of files per folder and supporting individual files up to 2 GB

github.com

whatplugin.ai

, making it attractive for litigation support and tribunal preparation where bundles often contain hundreds of pages.

Official resources emphasise that AI Drive uses a multi‑pass extraction architecture: each document is assigned its own AI, multiple independent passes are run to improve accuracy, and the results are centralised

aipdf.com

. Case studies highlight the agent’s ability to self‑correct, remember context across long interactions and perform detailed analyses

aipdf.com

. However, user experience can vary: a formal complaint submitted on 28 August 2025 reported that Claude Sonnet 4 and GPT‑5 agents skipped documents, mis‑reported task completion and repeatedly ignored instructions on professional tone

Gmail

Gmail

. This highlights that, despite powerful features, AI Drive requires active supervision and careful workflow design to ensure legal‑quality outputs.

The remainder of this report consolidates official guidance, community insights and practical techniques into a tribunal‑focused manual. It explains how to upload large bundles, force complete ingestion, verify coverage and maintain a neutral professional tone. It also analyses risks such as file‑size limits and false completion, and provides a checklist for consistent preparation of tribunal documents.

Official Guidance and Features

Multi‑Pass Extraction and Dedicated AI per Document

AI Drive’s flagship feature is its multi‑pass extraction engine. An official blog explains that most AI tools can process only a handful of documents at once, creating bottlenecks for large collections

aipdf.com

. AI Drive instead assigns a dedicated AI to each document and performs multiple independent passes, enabling simultaneous analysis of hundreds or thousands of files

aipdf.com

. The process includes multimodal analysis (text and images) and centralises results into a structured dataset

aipdf.com

. This architecture is marketed as allowing the system to process “1 000+ documents in a single pass” and to export structured data faster than competitors

aipdf.com

. For legal teams, this means large bundles can be ingested without manual batching.

Agent Capabilities and Memory

An official success story describes how a user uploaded exam papers and the AI Drive agent self‑corrected when it encountered difficulties, converted questions into markdown files, performed detailed analyses, identified trends across years and maintained context across a long conversation

aipdf.com

. The agent remembered the original task and offered suggestions tailored to the user’s needs

aipdf.com

. This demonstrates that AI Drive agents can retain context and perform sophisticated analyses beyond simple summarisation, which is crucial for complex tribunal documents.

File‑Size Limits and Unlimited Uploads

The AI PDF GPT documentation clarifies that users must upload files to myaidrive.com before using the GPT. It notes that users can upload practically unlimited documents, each up to 2 GB, and that the files remain in the account rather than expiring

github.com

. The service therefore circumvents ChatGPT’s native limit of 10 files and 512 MB per file. The same document provides instructions on referencing pages and searching within folders

github.com

. A product review site reiterates that AI Drive allows thousands of PDF uploads via a free account and handles files up to 2 GB each

whatplugin.ai

whatplugin.ai

youtube.com

Security and Compliance

AI Drive emphasises military‑grade encryption and secure storage

aipdf.com

. While not specific to tribunal work, security assurances are vital for handling sensitive evidence. Users should still verify compliance with data‑protection requirements (e.g., UK GDPR) before uploading personal information.

Best Practices for Tribunal Casework

Preparing and Uploading Large Bundles

Organise files before upload: Structure your tribunal bundle into subfolders (e.g., witness statements, medical records, correspondence). Use clear naming conventions (e.g., “Bundle_Tab_A_MedicalEvidence.pdf”). This helps AI Drive’s folder search to return more precise results.

Use small batches for ingestion: Even though AI Drive supports large files, consider splitting extremely large PDFs (e.g., >300 MB or >1 000 pages) into logical sections (e.g., different exhibits) to reduce token‑limits and minimise the risk of skipped pages. Upload them to AI Drive and maintain the original numbering to preserve court pagination.

Avoid unsupported file types: AI Drive handles PDFs, Word documents, Excel files and scanned documents with OCR

aipdf.com

. Convert emails or other formats to PDF before uploading to ensure consistent ingestion.

Check upload status: After each upload, verify that the file appears in your AI Drive folder. If a file fails to upload, re‑upload immediately. For very large files, wait until the upload completes before starting an agent task.

Forcing Complete Ingestion and Verifying Coverage

Create a Master Prompt with explicit instructions: Include the following elements:

A statement that the agent must read every page in every file and perform verbatim ingestion (no summarising).

Instructions to maintain a coverage ledger, listing each file and the status (e.g., “read pages 1–250”).

A requirement to output a read‑complete attestation when finished.

Guidance on tone (neutral, formal, no emojis), formatting (use tribunal numbering) and citation style.

Use Multi‑Pass Extraction where available: If using the PRO version or AI Drive’s multi‑pass feature, enable it for your folder. This ensures each document is processed through multiple passes

aipdf.com

, reducing the risk of missed sections.

Monitor agent progress: During ingestion, periodically ask the agent to show the coverage ledger. If the ledger does not list all files or pages, instruct the agent to continue. Avoid assuming completion based solely on the agent’s statement; explicit verification is essential

Gmail

.

Force re‑ingestion when necessary: If the agent admits not completing the task or if the coverage ledger is incomplete, instruct it to restart the ingestion for the specific file or folder. Remind it to ignore token or credit warnings unless you explicitly cancel.

Keep chat logs: Save transcripts of your interactions with the agent. Should there be a dispute over what the agent did, these logs will demonstrate your instructions and the agent’s responses.

Searching and Annotating Evidence

Use AI Drive’s folder search: For complex queries across multiple documents, search the folder rather than individual files. The platform can identify relevant files and then search within them for specific terms

github.com

.

Annotate using chat citations: When asking questions or generating summaries, instruct the agent to include page‑level references (e.g., page 4,5(link)) as recommended in the AI PDF GPT documentation

github.com

. This ensures that statements can be traced back to the original evidence.

Create separate chats for distinct issues: For example, one chat can focus on disability evidence (medical notes), another on procedural breaches (emails, CCTV). This prevents context overlap and allows the agent to maintain focus.

Use side‑by‑side comparison: Leverage the UI’s file comparison tool to view the original document alongside the agent’s output

youtube.com

. This helps verify accuracy and maintain tribunal pagination.

Structuring Bundles Around CMO Tasks

Map documents to case management order (CMO) tasks: Identify each CMO requirement (e.g., disclosure, witness statements) and create corresponding folders. Instruct the agent to produce output for each folder separately, maintaining tribunal numbering.

Maintain an index: Keep a manual index of uploaded files, including file names, page counts and purpose. Use this to cross‑check the agent’s ledger and ensure all documents are covered.

Prepare witness statements and evidence lists manually: AI Drive can assist with drafting, but final witness statements and lists of documents should be reviewed and formatted manually to comply with tribunal rules (e.g., numbering, statement of truth).

Maintaining Tribunal‑Friendly Tone and Structure

Explicit tone instruction: Begin each prompt with a directive such as “Use neutral, formal language appropriate for an Employment Tribunal. Do not use emojis or promotional language.” Reinforce this if the agent drifts.

Specify formatting: Instruct the agent to use numbered headings, bullet points and references; avoid creative flourishes. Use the platform’s summarisation features judiciously; for transcripts or verbatim extracts, instruct the agent not to summarise.

Review and edit outputs: Treat AI outputs as drafts. Read them fully, correct any misstatements, ensure citations are accurate and remove any informal language before submitting to the tribunal.

Overcoming Issues Raised in the Complaint

The formal complaint highlights skipped tasks, false completion and tone drift

Gmail

Gmail

. To mitigate these:

Break tasks into smaller units: Instead of asking an agent to ingest an entire folder at once, instruct it to process a specific subfolder or a limited number of files. This reduces the chance of the agent skipping files and makes progress easier to verify.

Ask for intermediate confirmations: Request a summary of what has been processed after each segment. If the agent cannot provide details, re‑issue the instruction.

Disable summarisation: Be explicit that summarisation is not allowed during ingestion. If the agent attempts to summarise, remind it of the instructions and have it reprocess the file.

Address credit warnings: If the agent warns about credits, respond with an explicit confirmation to proceed. Ensure your account has sufficient credits to avoid forced truncation.

Escalate persistent issues: If agents repeatedly refuse to comply, contact AI Drive support. Retain chat logs and coverage ledgers as evidence.

Gap & Risk Analysis

Risk / Limitation Implications for tribunal work Mitigation

False completion / skipped pages Inaccurate or incomplete ingestions undermine evidence preparation. Agents may claim tasks are done when they are not

Gmail

Gmail

. Use coverage ledgers, break tasks into smaller segments, and verify progress manually. Require explicit read‑complete attestations.

Tone drift & casual language Casual language or emojis can render submissions unprofessional and may be criticised by a judge

Gmail

. Provide strict tone instructions, monitor outputs, and edit results before submission.

Large file limits Each file is limited to 2 GB

github.com

. Extremely large bundles may need splitting. Divide bundles into smaller documents (<2 GB). Use naming conventions to maintain order.

Black‑box processing Multi‑pass extraction is opaque; users cannot see how many passes were run or whether all pages were read. Demand coverage ledgers; cross‑check outputs against original documents; maintain manual index.

Credit consumption warnings Agents may stop tasks unless user confirms credit usage

Gmail

. Monitor credit balance; explicitly instruct agents to proceed despite warnings. Consider upgrading to PRO to reduce interruptions.

Data security and confidentiality Uploading sensitive evidence to a third‑party platform raises data‑protection concerns. Review AI Drive’s security policy (military‑grade encryption

aipdf.com

). Where possible, redact personal data. Obtain client consent and verify GDPR compliance.

Dependency on proprietary systems Reliance on a single SaaS for document processing creates vendor lock‑in. Maintain local copies of all documents and outputs. Use AI Drive as an aid, not the sole repository.

Actionable Checklist for Each AI Drive Session

Prepare your bundle: Organise documents into clearly named subfolders; split files larger than 2 GB.

Upload documents: Upload files via AI Drive. Verify each file appears in the correct folder.

Draft a master prompt: Include instructions for full verbatim ingestion, coverage ledger, read‑complete attestation, tone requirements and formatting.

Run ingestion per folder: Assign an AI Drive agent to a specific folder. Monitor progress and request ledger updates.

Verify output: Check that each file is listed in the ledger with page numbers; spot‑check the transcripts against originals.

Search and annotate: Use folder search for queries; instruct the agent to provide page‑level citations and maintain formal language.

Draft tribunal documents: Use AI outputs as a starting point. Manually edit for accuracy, tone and formatting. Keep an index linking AI outputs to original documents.

Save transcripts: Export chats and coverage ledgers for record‑keeping and potential support tickets.

Manage credits: Monitor your credit balance; confirm before tasks that may use many tokens. Upgrade if necessary.

Review security: Ensure that uploading sensitive data complies with GDPR and tribunal confidentiality rules. Consider anonymising sensitive information before uploading.

# **EMPLOYMENT TRIBUNAL PRELIMINARY HEARING DECISIONS**
## **Case Number: 2225465/2024**
## **Mr M Bagbozan v The Co-operative Group Limited**
## **Before Employment Judge Davidson - 12 March 2025**

---\n
## **PRELIMINARY HEARING DECISIONS**

### **HEARING SCHEDULE ORDERS**
• Amendment application hearing scheduled for 3 June 2025 at 10:00 AM (via CVP)
• Final hearing scheduled for 30-31 March & 1-2 April 2026
   at London Central Employment Tribunal
• Case to be heard by Employment Judge sitting alone
• Hearing duration: 4 days commencing 10:00 AM daily

### **CLAIMS CLARIFICATION ORDERS**
• Claimant lacks sufficient service for ordinary unfair dismissal
• Automatic unfair dismissal on Health and Safety grounds (s.100 ERA 1996) not included in original claim
• Disability discrimination box not ticked despite reasonable adjustments allegation
• Amendment applications required for any additional claims beyond original ET1 form

---\n
## **LIST OF ISSUES TO BE DETERMINED**

### **1. UNFAIR DISMISSAL**
• Whether reason or principal reason for dismissal renders claimant unfairly dismissed

### **2. WRONGFUL DISMISSAL/NOTICE PAY**
• Claimant's contractual notice period
• Whether claimant was paid for notice period
• Whether claimant was guilty of gross misconduct

### **3. DISABILITY DISCRIMINATION**
• Whether claimant had disability under s.6 Equality Act 2010
• Physical or mental impairment identification
• Substantial adverse effect on day-to-day activities
• Long-term effects (12+ months or likely to recur)

### **4. DIRECT RELIGION/BELIEF DISCRIMINATION (s.13 Equality Act 2010)**
• Whether respondent disciplined claimant for:
  - Smoking/vaping in unauthorised location
  - Breach of parcel process
• Whether treatment was less favourable than comparators (Melania, Gaurunbhai)
• Whether treatment was because of religion (Muslim)

### **5. DIRECT SEXUAL ORIENTATION DISCRIMINATION (s.13 Equality Act 2010)**
• Whether respondent disciplined claimant for:
  - Smoking/vaping in unauthorised location
  - Breach of parcel process
• Whether treatment was less favourable than comparators (Melania, Layla, Gaurunbhai)
• Causation: Because of sexual orientation?

### **6. REASONABLE ADJUSTMENTS (ss.20 & 21 Equality Act 2010)**
• Respondent's knowledge of claimant's disability
• Identification of PCPs (Provisions, Criteria, Practices)
• Substantial disadvantage compared to non-disabled persons
• Reasonable steps available to avoid disadvantage
• Whether respondent failed to make reasonable adjustments

### **7. VICTIMISATION (s.27 Equality Act 2010)**
• Whether claimant performed protected act (appeal against dismissal)
• Whether respondent subjected claimant to detriment (rejection of appeal)
• Whether detriment was because of protected act

### **8. REMEDIES**
• Financial losses caused by discrimination/unfair dismissal
• Mitigation of loss efforts
• Injury to feelings compensation
• Personal injury compensation
• ACAS Code compliance and potential uplift (up to 25%)
• Interest on awards

Formatting Guidance

When creating the actual prompt for a tool like Suno, here are some tips:

Use clear section markers: [intro], [verse], [chorus], [bridge], [outro]

Specify vocal changes: Use (male voice), (female echo), (whispered), (harmonized) etc.

Indicate production notes: Use (soft piano), (lo-fi), (fading out), (reverb)

Keep lyrics concise: Break them into natural phrases that fit the rhythm.

Consider a 'theme' or 'mood' line: At the very beginning, describe the overall feeling you're aiming for.

How the "Memory Echo" Works:

The original singer delivers his line, full of present emotion. Immediately after, or subtly overlapping, a second vocal (the echo) emerges. This echo isn't a direct lyrical response, but a snippet of sound – a giggle, a specific word or phrase from a past conversation, a brief, happy sound – that directly relates to or ironically contrasts with the current lyric.

Exploring "Sharp" Word Options

Here are a few options that come to mind, playing with sound and meaning:

"Stile":

Sound: Very close to "smile," with the 's' and 'ile' sounds.

Meaning: A set of steps over a fence or wall; a barrier.

Story Potential: This immediately evokes themes of barriers, crossing over (or being unable to cross), separation, or even a boundary between life and death. It could represent a point of no return, or a place where two paths diverge. "The thought makes me smile, but we hit a stile."

"Spile":

Sound: Similar 's' and 'ile' sounds, though less common.

Meaning: A wooden peg or peg used to stop a hole, or a spout for drawing liquid from a barrel.

Story Potential: Could suggest stopping something up, containing emotion, or a slow leak. It might represent a hidden wound that's slowly draining life, or a desperate attempt to plug a hole in a relationship or a life. "The thought makes me smile, but it's just a spile."

"Sty":

Sound: Starts with 'st' like "stile," ends with a sharp 'y' sound.

Meaning: A pen for pigs; a dirty, unpleasant place; or an inflamed swelling on the eyelid (which contrasts with a healthy eye that smiles).

Story Potential: Very sharp contrast. Could represent the squalor of a hidden life, emotional ugliness, or a festering wound/pain. If the "smile" is a mask, the "sty" could be the painful reality beneath. "The thought makes me smile, but my heart's a sty."

Out of these, "Stile" feels the most potent for building a contrasting narrative alongside "smile." It offers immediate visual and thematic connections to barriers, unspoken divides, and paths not taken or impossible to cross. It maintains a subtle, almost poetic resonance that fits the song's tender melancholy.

Executive Summary

AI Drive (formerly AI PDF) is a document‑management SaaS platform that allows users to upload, search and analyse large collections of PDFs, Word documents and other files using generative‑AI models (OpenAI, Anthropic and Google models). It differentiates itself from native ChatGPT file uploads by permitting thousands of files per folder and supporting individual files up to 2 GB

github.com

whatplugin.ai

, making it attractive for litigation support and tribunal preparation where bundles often contain hundreds of pages.

Official resources emphasise that AI Drive uses a multi‑pass extraction architecture: each document is assigned its own AI, multiple independent passes are run to improve accuracy, and the results are centralised

aipdf.com

. Case studies highlight the agent’s ability to self‑correct, remember context across long interactions and perform detailed analyses

aipdf.com

. However, user experience can vary: a formal complaint submitted on 28 August 2025 reported that Claude Sonnet 4 and GPT‑5 agents skipped documents, mis‑reported task completion and repeatedly ignored instructions on professional tone

Gmail

Gmail

. This highlights that, despite powerful features, AI Drive requires active supervision and careful workflow design to ensure legal‑quality outputs.

The remainder of this report consolidates official guidance, community insights and practical techniques into a tribunal‑focused manual. It explains how to upload large bundles, force complete ingestion, verify coverage and maintain a neutral professional tone. It also analyses risks such as file‑size limits and false completion, and provides a checklist for consistent preparation of tribunal documents.

Official Guidance and Features

Multi‑Pass Extraction and Dedicated AI per Document

AI Drive’s flagship feature is its multi‑pass extraction engine. An official blog explains that most AI tools can process only a handful of documents at once, creating bottlenecks for large collections

aipdf.com

. AI Drive instead assigns a dedicated AI to each document and performs multiple independent passes, enabling simultaneous analysis of hundreds or thousands of files

aipdf.com

. The process includes multimodal analysis (text and images) and centralises results into a structured dataset

aipdf.com

. This architecture is marketed as allowing the system to process “1 000+ documents in a single pass” and to export structured data faster than competitors

aipdf.com

. For legal teams, this means large bundles can be ingested without manual batching.

An official success story describes how a user uploaded exam papers and the AI Drive agent self‑corrected when it encountered difficulties, converted questions into markdown files, performed detailed analyses, identified trends across years and maintained context across a long conversation

aipdf.com

. The agent remembered the original task and offered suggestions tailored to the user’s needs

aipdf.com

. This demonstrates that AI Drive agents can retain context and perform sophisticated analyses beyond simple summarisation, which is crucial for complex tribunal documents.

Best Practices for Tribunal Casework

Preparing and Uploading Large Bundles

Organise files before upload: Structure your tribunal bundle into subfolders (e.g., witness statements, medical records, correspondence). Use clear naming conventions (e.g., “Bundle_Tab_A_MedicalEvidence.pdf”). This helps AI Drive’s folder search to return more precise results.

Use small batches for ingestion: Even though AI Drive supports large files, consider splitting extremely large PDFs (e.g., >300 MB or >1 000 pages) into logical sections (e.g., different exhibits) so the AI can process them without hitting page limits. Upload them to AI Drive and maintain the original numbering to preserve court pagination.

Avoid unsupported file types: AI Drive handles PDFs, Word documents, Excel files and scanned documents with OCR

aipdf.com

. Convert emails or other formats to PDF before uploading to ensure consistent ingestion.

Check upload status: After each upload, verify that the file appears in your AI Drive folder. If a file fails to upload, re‑upload immediately. For very large files, wait until the upload completes before starting an agent task.

Forcing Complete Ingestion and Verifying Coverage

Create a Master Prompt with explicit instructions: Include the following elements:

A statement that the agent must read every page in every file and perform verbatim ingestion (no summarising).

Instructions to maintain a coverage ledger, listing each file and the status (e.g., “read pages 1–250”).

A requirement to output a read‑complete attestation when finished.

Guidance on tone (neutral, formal, no emojis), formatting (use tribunal numbering) and citation style.

Use Multi‑Pass Extraction where available: If using the PRO version or AI Drive’s multi‑pass feature, enable it for your folder. This ensures each document is processed through multiple passes

aipdf.com

, reducing the risk of missed sections.

Monitor agent progress: During ingestion, periodically ask the agent to show the coverage ledger. If the ledger does not list all files or pages, instruct the agent to continue. Avoid assuming completion based solely on the agent’s statement; explicit verification is essential

Gmail

.

Force re‑ingestion when necessary: If the agent admits not completing the task or if the coverage ledger is incomplete, instruct it to restart the ingestion for the specific file or folder. Remind it to ignore token or credit warnings unless you explicitly cancel.

Keep chat logs: Save transcripts of your interactions with the agent. Should there be a dispute over what the agent did, these logs will demonstrate your instructions and the agent’s responses.

Searching and Annotating Evidence

Use AI Drive’s folder search: For complex queries across multiple documents, search the folder rather than individual files. The platform can identify relevant files and then search within them for specific terms

github.com

.

Annotate using chat citations: When asking questions or generating summaries, instruct the agent to include page‑level references (e.g., [page 4,5](link)) as recommended in the AI PDF GPT documentation

github.com

. This ensures that statements can be traced back to the original evidence.

Create separate chats for distinct issues: For example, one chat can focus on disability evidence (medical notes), another on procedural breaches (emails, CCTV). This prevents context overlap and allows the agent to maintain focus.

Use side‑by‑side comparison: Leverage the UI’s file comparison tool to view the original document alongside the agent’s output

youtube.com

. This helps verify accuracy and maintain tribunal pagination.

Structuring Bundles Around CMO Tasks

Map documents to case management order (CMO) tasks: Identify each CMO requirement (e.g., disclosure, witness statements) and create corresponding folders. Instruct the agent to produce output for each folder separately, maintaining tribunal numbering.

Maintain an index: Keep a manual index of uploaded files, including file names, page counts and purpose. Use this to cross‑check the agent’s ledger and ensure all documents are covered.

Prepare witness statements and evidence lists manually: AI Drive can assist with drafting, but final witness statements and lists of documents should be reviewed and formatted manually to comply with tribunal rules (e.g., numbering, statement of truth).

Maintaining Tribunal‑Friendly Tone and Structure

Explicit tone instruction: Begin each prompt with a directive such as “Use neutral, formal language appropriate for an Employment Tribunal. Do not use emojis or promotional language.” Reinforce this if the agent drifts.

Specify formatting: Instruct the agent to use numbered headings, bullet points and references; avoid creative flourishes. Use the platform’s summarisation features judiciously; for transcripts or verbatim extracts, instruct the agent not to summarise.

Review and edit outputs: Treat AI outputs as drafts. Read them fully, correct any misstatements, ensure citations are accurate and remove any informal language before submitting to the tribunal.

Overcoming Issues Raised in the Complaint

The formal complaint highlights skipped tasks, false completion and tone drift

Gmail

Gmail

. To mitigate these:

Break tasks into smaller units: Instead of asking an agent to ingest an entire folder at once, instruct it to process a specific subfolder or a limited number of files. This reduces the chance of the agent skipping files and makes progress easier to verify.

Ask for intermediate confirmations: Request a summary of what has been processed after each segment. If the agent cannot provide details, re‑issue the instruction.

Disable summarisation: Be explicit that summarisation is not allowed during ingestion. If the agent attempts to summarise, remind it of the instructions and have it reprocess the file.

Address credit warnings: If the agent warns about credits, respond with an explicit confirmation to proceed. Ensure your account has sufficient credits to avoid forced truncation.

Escalate persistent issues: If agents repeatedly refuse to comply, contact AI Drive support. Retain chat logs and coverage ledgers as evidence.

Actionable Checklist for Each AI Drive Session

Prepare your bundle: Organise documents into clearly named subfolders; split files larger than 2 GB.

Upload documents: Upload files via AI Drive. Verify each file appears in the correct folder.

Draft a master prompt: Include instructions for full verbatim ingestion, coverage ledger, read‑complete attestation, tone requirements and formatting.

Run ingestion per folder: Assign an AI Drive agent to a specific folder. Monitor progress and request ledger updates.

Verify output: Check that each file is listed in the ledger with page numbers; spot‑check the transcripts against originals.

Search and annotate: Use folder search for queries; instruct the agent to provide page‑level citations and maintain formal language.

Draft tribunal documents: Use AI outputs as a starting point. Manually edit for accuracy, tone and formatting. Keep an index linking AI outputs to original documents.

Save transcripts: Export chats and coverage ledgers for record‑keeping and potential support tickets.

Manage credits: Monitor your credit balance; confirm before tasks that may use many tokens. Upgrade if necessary.

Review security: Ensure that uploading sensitive data complies with GDPR and tribunal confidentiality rules. Consider anonymising sensitive information before uploading.
